title: Variables and Graphs
text:
Variables
A variable is a symbol (e.g., X) that can assume any of a prescribed set of values, called the domain of the variable. A variable that can only assume a single value is known as a constant (e.g., Avogadro’s constant: 6.02214076 × 10²³). On the other hand, if a variable can theoretically assume any value between two given values, then it is a continuous variable, otherwise it is called a discrete variable.
For example, for the Number G gallons (gal) of water in a washing machine, the variable G can assume any value between 0 gal (no water) to the capacity of the washing machine. As such, the variable G is continuous. By contrast, for the Number B of books on a library shelf, the variable B is discrete as it can only take on discrete values such as 0,1,2,3,… to the maximum number of books that can fit on the shelf.
What about for Country C in Europe? In this case, the variable C is a discrete (nominal) variable and can take on values such as France or Germany, which may be represented numerically (e.g., France = 1, Germany = 2).


Rounding of Data
Some rounding procedures are more commonly used in statistics and scientific computing than others, particularly because they can help minimise systematic bias and cumulative rounding errors. For example, take the numbers 4.35, 8.65, 2.95, 12.45, 6.65, 7.55 and 9.75. In summing them directly, we obtain:

 num_list = c(4.35, 8.65, 2.95, 12.45, 6.65, 7.55, 9.75)
 sum_num_list = sum(num_list)
 print(sum_num_list)

[1] 52.35


We can also first round the numbers to the nearest tenth according to the “round-to-even” convention (which is default in R but can be interrupted by floating-point precision, hence we have to write a custom rounding function to get a traditional “round-to-even” output ). Using this procedure, any digit before 5 is rounded to the nearest even integer. In applying this rounding procedure, we obtain:


# Create a custom function for standard rounding
bankers_round <- function(x, digits = 1) {
  scale <- 10^digits
  round(x * scale) / scale
}

# Apply the function
rounded_to_even_num_list <- bankers_round(num_list,1)

print(rounded_to_even_num_list)

[1]  4.4  8.6  3.0 12.4  6.6  7.6  9.8


Summing these “rounded-to-even” numbers, gives us:


sum_rounded_to_even_num_list <-  sum(rounded_to_even_num_list)
print(sum_rounded_to_even_num_list)

[1] 52.4


Another rounding method “round-half-up” is to increase the digit before 5. In applying this procedure, we get:


# Round up
rounded_up_num_list <- ceiling(num_list * 10) / 10

#Sum the resulting numbers
sum_rounded_up_num_list <- sum(rounded_up_num_list)
print(sum_rounded_up_num_list)

[1] 52.7


We can see here that using the “round-half-up” method produced a result of 52.7, while the “round-to-even” method produced a result of 52.4, which has a smaller cumulative rounding error relative to the direct sum of 52.35.
While the round-to-even method can help reduce systematic rounding bias by allowing upward and downward rounding errors to balance each other out, it does not guarantee that cumulative rounding errors will cancel out, particularly when rounding errors occur predominantly in one direction.


Functions and Graphs
We can write functions in R to perform mathematical operations. Base R also supports vectorisation, whereby an operation can be applied to each element of a vector without the need to explicitly write loops.

For example, take the linear equation
\[
Y = 4X - 4
\]
This relationship can be expressed mathematically as \(Y = F(X)\) , where to each value that X can assume, there corresponds one and only one value of Y.
In R, this relationship can be represented using a function:

# Computes a linear transformation over an entire vector simultaneously 
linear_func <- function(X) {
  Y <- 4*X - 4
  return(Y)
}

# Generate a number sequuence to which we apply the linear transformation
num_seq <- c(-5:5)

# Apply the fucntion to the number sequence
linear_eq_result <- linear_func(num_seq)

We can also graph the equation as follows:

# Combine X and Y into a dataset to make plotting easier
df_linear_plot <- data.frame(x = num_seq, y = linear_eq_result)

library(ggplot2)

ggplot(data = df_linear_plot, aes(x = x, y = y)) + geom_point(size = 2, alpha = 0.5) + geom_line() + theme_minimal()








We can also graph a quadratic equation, which will give us a parabolic curve:

# Computes a quadratic transformation over an entire vector simultaneously 
quadratic_func <- function(X) {
  Y <- 2*X^2 - 3*X - 9
  return(Y)
}

# Generate a number sequuence to which we apply the quadratic transformation
num_seq <- c(-5:5)

# Apply the fucntion to the number sequence
quadratic_eq_result <- quadratic_func(num_seq)

# Combine X and Y into a dataset to make plotting easier
df_quadratic_plot <- data.frame(x = num_seq, y = quadratic_eq_result)

ggplot(data = df_quadratic_plot, aes(x = x, y = y)) + geom_point(size = 2, alpha = 0.5) + geom_line() + theme_minimal()








Plots are also helpful to visualise and explore relationships between variables in real-world scenarios. For example, let’s simulate a small dataset showing the rise in new diabetes diagnoses from 1997 to 2005.


#n Specify variables
year <- c(1997:2005)
millions <- c(0.88,0.90,1.01,1.10,1.20,1.25,1.28,1.36,1.41)

# Combine variables into df to make it easier to plot
diabetes_rate <- data.frame(year = year, millions = millions)

# Plot the data as a time series to clearly show the trend of rising diabetes diagnoses from 1997 to 205
ggplot(data = diabetes_rate, aes(x= year, y = millions)) + geom_point(size = 2, alpha = 0.5) + geom_line() + xlab("Year") + ylab("Number of diabetes diagnoses (millions)") + theme_minimal()








But what if we have data that grow exponentially? For example, suppose we are investigating the growth of an infectious disease over 30 days, assuming that the number of cases increases by approximately 20% each day. By simulating these data in R, we obtain the following:


set.seed(123)

days <- 1:30

cases <- 10 * 1.2^(days - 1) *
  exp(rnorm(30, mean = 0, sd = 0.15))

epidemic_data <- data.frame(days, cases)

print(epidemic_data)

   days       cases
1     1    9.193657
2     2   11.592751
3     3   18.192955
4     4   17.463728
5     5   21.142061
6     6   32.183459
7     7   31.997311

10   10   48.261291
11   11   74.396800
12   12   78.421199
13   13   94.685369
14   14  108.784378
15   15  118.121141
16   16  201.430703
17   17  199.219568
18   18  165.183832
19   19  295.768336
20   20  297.607636
21   21  326.634782
22   22  445.252505
23   23  473.313839
24   24  593.862146
25   25  723.822767
26   26  740.718022
27   27 1298.043781
28   28 1405.675282
29   29 1389.734697
30   30 2387.453219


If we plot this data on a regular linear scale, we obtain:


ggplot(data = epidemic_data, aes(x= days, y =cases)) + geom_point(size = 2, alpha = 0.5) + geom_line() + theme_minimal()








Notice that due to the large variation in y-values, the data points on the left-hand side of the plot appear compressed, making it difficult to distinguish differences between individual observations. For example, the absolute increase between days 29 and 30 is approximately 997 cases, compared to an increase of only 3 cases between days 1 and 2. Consequently, the larger absolute differences towards the later days of the epidemic are much easier to visualise, while the smaller differences during the earlier days are less apparent.
However, when examining epidemic growth, we may be interested not only in absolute differences but also in relative changes (e.g., percentage increases) over time. One way to better visualise these relative changes is to use a semi-log plot, where the y-axis is represented on a logarithmic scale. Unlike a linear scale, where equal distances represent equal absolute differences, equal distances on a logarithmic scale represent equal ratios. This makes it easier to compare proportional changes across observations of different magnitudes.

ggplot(epidemic_data, aes(x = days, y = cases)) + geom_line() + geom_point() + scale_y_log10() + xlab("Day") + ylab("Number of cases (log10 scale)") + theme_minimal()








When the number of cases is plotted on a logarithmic scale, the previously curved relationship appears approximately linear. This suggests that the number of cases is increasing at a relatively constant proportional rate over time, consistent with exponential growth. Although the absolute increase in cases becomes progressively larger, the relative rate of increase remains approximately constant, as reflected by the roughly linear trend on the semi-log plot.

title: Welcome to TomatoData
text:
Hi, my name is Vina Thanabalan. I recently graduated with a PhD in cognitive neuroscience. My research focused on analysing neuroimaging (fMRI) data to better understand how the human brain comprehends language beyond lab settings and in the real world, such as while watching movies!
After my PhD, I realised that what I loved even more than brains was statistics. Now, I work for a not-for-profit organisation doing research and evaluation work with community service and public health data.

title: Welcome to TomatoData
text:
About TomatoData
I created TomatoData to document my learnings in statistics and to showcase various projects related to epidemiology and biostatistics.
I chose tomatoes because, much like my love for statistics, my fondness for them grew over time. 🍅
